catalog_quote: Mano has three level tones, low (kɛ̀ɛ̀ ‘year’), mid (kɛ̄ ‘in order to’), and high (kɛ́í ‘refuse’). Extra-high tone is marginal in the system, as it appears only in ideophones, expressive adverbs, and interjections ... The tone-bearing unit is a vowel or a syllabic nasal; long vowels and diphthongs are considered combinations of phonemes. Complex tonal contours appear only on VV sequences. All tonal combinations are possible (see Table 3). Unlike some Southwestern Mande languages, such as Kpelle (Konoshenko 2014), no tonal spreading occurs in Mano, and grammatical tonal marking is hosted by specific words rather than phrases. Furthermore, Mano does not have stress accent, which is often (but not always) the case for tonal languages (Hyman 2009). Utterance-level prosodic operations include the lowering of the tone on final vowels in affirmative utterances and a general downdrift. || Mande…
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files present under with. (1) Primary: Helda reprint of Linguistic Typology 25(1), CC BY). PDF page 8 = journal p.129, sec. 3.2 'Suprasegmental phonology' contains, verbatim: 'Mano has three level tones, low (kɛ̀ɛ̀ 'year'), mid (kɛ̄ 'in order to'), and high (kɛ́í 'refuse').. Unlike some Southwestern Mande languages, such as Kpelle (Konoshenko 2014), no tonal spreading occurs in Mano, and grammatical tonal marking is hosted by specific words rather than phrases. Furthermore, Mano does not have stress accent, which is often (but not always) the case for tonal languages (Hyman 2009). Utterance-level prosodic operations include the lowering of the tone on final vowels in affirmative utterances…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mano is a three-level tone language (L/M/H, all contour combinations on vowel sequences, marginal extra-high) with no word stress/stress accent according to its describer; the only sub-word prosodic constituent is the 'metric foot' (V, CV(ŋ), CVV, CVCV(ŋ)), a domain of vowel harmony, consonant-distribution restrictions and grammatical tone replacement, not of prominence. The grammar notes only indirect within-foot asymmetry (the first vowel of CVlV / some CV1V2 feet may reduce in fast speech, i.e. if anything the non-initial vowel is the stable one).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None (no stress at all per source).
new_statements.exceptions: English loanwords in Liberian Mano keep the English stress pattern (deZeeuw & Kruah 1981); fast-speech reduction of the first vowel in CVlV feet (CVlV > ClV) noted as indirect vowel asymmetry (Khachaturyan 2015: 25 fn.12, §1.8).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word/lexical level; phrase-level prosody consists of downdrift and utterance-final tone lowering (affirmatives) and raised register/final rise in questions. Description based mainly on Guinean Mano (Nzérékoré area; Maa/Zan dialects), which the author treats as one language with Liberian Mano.
new_statements.identity_note: All three quoted statements are by the same describer (M. Khachaturyan) and rest primarily on Guinean Mano (máá, Nzérékoré prefecture; Maa, Zan/Yassédou dialects), which Glottolog subsumes under mann1248 'Mann' (ISO mev) together with Liberian Mano (Nimba County). deZeeuw & Kruah 1981 and Schwab 1947 describe Liberian Mano and say nothing about native word stress. No dialect-level glottocode distinction is needed; the language-level key mann1248 is correct.

new_statements.quote: p. 360: "While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned syllable in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable. Stress is acoustically marked by an increase in the loudness of the syllable and is often accompanied by a slight increase in the length of the syllable." [...] "No Mande language has more than three distinctive pitch levels. Kpelle and Mano have three: high, mid and low, while Lorma and Manya have two." — front matter p. [vi]: "Loan words generally reproduce the stress pattern of the English word, so that if you simply pronounce the word with its ordinary stress it will sound all right."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Lines 18351-18387 read, under the scanned page marker '360' and 'MANDE SUPRASEGMENTALS': sec. 2 Stress reads exactly 'While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is gener-ally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned sylla-ble in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable. Stress is acoustically marked by an increase in the loudness of the syllable and is often accompanied by a slight in-crease in the length of the syllable.'; sec. 3 Tone: 'No Mande language has more than three distinctive pitch levels. Kpelle and Mano have three: high, mid and low, while Lorma and Manya have two.' The puts this held by the project and maps leaf 372…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Khachaturyan 2021: 'Mano does not have stress accent'; 2017: 'Ударения в М.я. нет'): the handbook gives Mano no stress rule, treats word prosody as three level tones, and the Dwyer appendix calls Mande stress non-contrastive. It adds two details: English loanwords retain English stress, and a Mande-general phonetic prominence (loudness + length) is asserted, with placement stated only for Kpelle. It must not be read as a Mano placement rule; the Kpelle 'first high-toned syllable' rule is not claimed for Mano.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mano is presented as a three-level-tone language (high, mid, low; mid unmarked, with the mid-low interval small). The only stress statement is in Dwyer's Mande-general appendix: stress in Mande is 'generally non-contrastive' (a loudness/length prominence), and the placement rule given is for Kpelle (first high-toned syllable, else first syllable) — no placement rule is stated for Mano. The only Mano-specific remark on stress is that English loanwords keep their English stress pattern.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Mano. The appendix's 'generally distinctive' after 'generally non-contrastive' reads as a slip (presumably 'predictable'); the Kpelle rule is explicitly for Kpelle.
new_statements.identity_note: Dezeeuw & Kruah (1981) is based mainly on the 'lao maa' dialect (area west of Sacklepie north to Ganta, Nimba County, Liberia), with informants from other areas (introduction, 'Mano Dialects'); principal informant Rexanna Kruah of Yilah, Bong County. The stress paragraph itself is in David Dwyer's appendix on Liberian Mande languages generally and is illustrated with Kpelle, not Mano.
